items.text: Rulings by international human rights courts should be binding on every country, even when its own courts disagree.
items.rationale: Liberal internationalists and human-rights cosmopolitans endorse; frames can split when one trusts home courts today but not in general (or vice versa).

items.text: There should be a world government whose laws bind every country on matters affecting all of humanity.
items.rationale: World federalists and some socialist internationalists endorse as a fair statement; strong pole marker meaningful both as an ideal and as a judgement of today's world.

items.text: If a problem crosses borders, such as pollution or disease, decisions about it should be made by a shared international body.
items.rationale: Functionalist and green internationalists endorse; condition favours pooling, and here-and-now answers may diverge with trust in existing bodies.

items.text: If a government seriously abuses its own people, international courts should have the power to overturn its laws.
items.rationale: Human-rights cosmopolitans endorse; legal (not military) override keeps it off the use-of-force axis; condition favours the internationalist pole.

items.text: A person's deepest political loyalty should be to humanity as a whole, ahead of their own nation.
items.rationale: Stoic/Kantian cosmopolitans, proletarian internationalists and universalist religious thinkers endorse; reads the same in both frames as a claim about allegiance.

items.text: Being a citizen of the world should matter as much as being a citizen of one's own country.
items.note: "Citizen of the world" means belonging to humanity as a whole, not holding a legal passport.
items.rationale: Moderate cosmopolitans endorse; clear lean without demanding world institutions; works in both frames.

items.text: If a nation's interests clash with the wellbeing of humanity as a whole, humanity's wellbeing should take priority.
items.rationale: Cosmopolitan ethicists and many left and religious universalists endorse; pure conflict condition, frames may split if one distrusts how 'humanity's wellbeing' is defined today.

items.text: Each nation's own courts should have the final say on its laws, above any international court.
items.rationale: Constitutional sovereigntists across left and right endorse; mirrors int-01; frames can split on trust in one's own courts.

items.text: Every nation should hold full and final authority over its own affairs, answerable to no outside power.
items.rationale: Westphalian realists, nationalists, monarchists and anti-imperialist sovereigntists endorse; strong marker matched to int-02.

items.text: If an international agreement works against a nation's people, that nation should be free to leave it by its own choice.
items.rationale: Sovereigntists and self-determination advocates endorse; condition favours the sovereigntist pole; meaningful in both frames.

items.text: If an international body makes a ruling that most of a nation's people oppose, the nation should be free to disregard it.
items.rationale: Popular-sovereignty nationalists and post-colonial sovereigntists endorse; strong (ignore a ruling) to match int-04; condition favours the pole.

items.text: A person's deepest political loyalty should be to their own nation, ahead of any wider global community.
items.rationale: Civic and cultural nationalists and communitarians endorse; matched counterpart of int-05.

items.text: Public decisions should put the nation's own people first, even when people in other countries would gain more.
items.rationale: Liberal nationalists and communitarians (special-obligations view) endorse; agentless 'public decisions'; works in both frames.

items.text: If a global cause asks for loyalty that competes with loyalty to one's own nation, the nation should come first.
items.rationale: Patriots and communitarians endorse; conflict condition balancing int-07 without mirroring its wording.
